summary: In a courtroom scene from a fiction novel, the narrator Mr Yallow faces a judge after being arrested. Many detained people, held since a bridge bombing without trial, are being brought to court while the ACLU lawyer pleads for time. The judge considers holding Yallow for trial as a flight risk, but Yallow admits he stole a phone containing evidence about his friend Darryl Glover and gave it to a journalist, saying he chose to face justice rather than run. The judge grants bail, adds a petty theft charge, and sets an additional $50,000 bail.
one_line: Mr Yallow confronts a judge over his flight risk status and a stolen phone, and is granted bail with an added petty theft charge.
key_facts: Mr Yallow is brought before a judge who says the prosecution has identified him as a flight risk.
The judge says Yallow has more history than the other people in the courtroom.
Many of the prisoners had been locked up since the bridge blew and were taken for dead by their families.
Yallow says he could have run last week when someone offered to take him away and build him a new identity.
Yallow stole a woman's phone, escaped from their truck, and ran away.
The stolen phone had evidence about Yallow's friend, Darryl Glover, which Yallow gave to a journalist.
Yallow says he decided he could not run and had to face justice because his freedom meant nothing while his friends were still locked up.
Yallow admits he stole the phone and says he plans to give it back if he finds the young woman.
The judge says a video on the news that morning suggested Yallow had a legitimate reason to evade the authorities.
The judge grants bail and asks the prosecutor to add a charge of Misdemeanor Petty Theft regarding the phone.
The judge sets an additional bail of $50,000 for the petty theft charge.
The ACLU lawyer asked the judge for a few more hours while the prisoners' families were brought to the courthouse.
Yallow's lawyer is a woman who squeezes his hand after the bail decision.
The judge rapped his gavel and scrubbed at his eyes, appearing tired along with the lawyer and bailiffs.
